column6: About 20 mb/d of oil (a fifth of world consumption) and a fifth of world LNG, mostly from Qatar, pass here (EIA, 2024). Only Saudi Arabia's Petroline and the UAE's ADCOP pipeline can bypass it, and they can carry only a fraction of the flow.

Shortest sea link between the Indian Ocean and the Pacific: about 23 mb/d of oil in 2023, the most of any chokepoint (EIA). Most Gulf oil and LNG bound for China, Japan and Korea passes here; 2.7 km wide at the Phillips Channel off Singapore.

Gateway between the Gulf of Aden and the Red Sea, 26 km wide. About 8–9 mb/d of oil in 2023, roughly halved in 2024 after Houthi attacks on shipping pushed tankers and LNG carriers around Africa (EIA).

Suez Canal plus the parallel SUMED pipeline carried about 9 mb/d of oil and 8% of world LNG in 2023; traffic fell sharply in 2024 with the Red Sea crisis. Fully laden supertankers are too deep for the canal and unload part of their cargo into SUMED.
14 km wide link between the Mediterranean and the Atlantic: Algerian, Libyan and Black Sea exports heading west, and Atlantic cargoes for southern Europe, including those rerouted round the Cape.
The Great Belt and Øresund are the only exit from the Baltic for Russia's Primorsk and Ust-Luga ports, about 3–5 mb/d of oil. Closely watched for Russia's 'shadow fleet' of ageing tankers.

Not a strait but the only alternative to Suez between Asia and Europe. Tanker and LNG traffic round the Cape jumped in 2024 when shippers avoided the Red Sea, adding 10–14 days to a Gulf–Europe voyage.
Used mainly by US LNG and petroleum products heading to Asia; too narrow for supertankers. The 2023–24 drought cut daily transits and pushed many LNG carriers round the Cape instead.
The Bosphorus and Dardanelles are the only sea exit from the Black Sea: about 3–4 mb/d of Russian, Kazakh and Azeri oil, through a channel 700 m wide at its narrowest in central Istanbul.
Explosions on 26 September 2022 ruptured three of the four Nord Stream strings north-east and south-east of Bornholm.
